opus-5.5.text:
I think the comparative advantage of people in this community has always been a willingness to take weird, high-stakes possibilities seriously before there's consensus that they're real. Ten years ago, saying "AI could transform everything within our lifetimes" sounded fringe. Now a lot of the world has caught up to that framing. So I think the role shifts a bit.

One part of it is to keep doing the thing that got us here: staying ahead of the curve. What's the next set of questions that seem speculative now but will feel obvious in three or five years? Things like: what happens when AI systems are doing most of the AI research? How would we know if we're in a fast takeoff versus a gradual one? What does it look like for AI systems to have meaningful autonomy in the economy? Those are the questions where someone comfortable reasoning under deep uncertainty can add a lot, because institutions tend not to touch them until they're forced to.

But the other part, which I've come to care about more, is translation and grounding. Being comfortable with speculation can become a liability if it means you're not checking your views against reality. I'd love to see more people take their big-picture worldviews and turn them into concrete, falsifiable predictions, or into evaluations and benchmarks that would tell us whether some scary capability is actually arriving. If you think AI R&D automation is the crux, help build the measurements that would show it coming. That's how you get people who don't share your priors to update. They won't be moved by an argument from first principles, but they might be moved by a clear trend line.

And I think there's real value in being honest brokers. A lot of discourse around AI is polarized between "this is all hype" and "we're definitely doomed." People who can hold genuine uncertainty, say "here's what I'd expect to see if I'm wrong," and engage respectfully with skeptics are pretty rare. That kind of epistemic posture is a contribution in itself, maybe especially to policymakers trying to figure out who to trust.

So: keep exploring the frontier of strange questions, but tether those explorations to evidence and communicate them in a way that's legible to people outside the bubble.

r001.rationale: It recommends exploring speculative questions where institutions tend not to engage until forced, saying people comfortable with deep uncertainty can add a lot.

r002.rationale: It recommends research-related work alongside translation, evidence-based communication, and engaging with skeptics; it does not say the contribution should be heavily concentrated on research.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, because I feel like the EA community's comparative advantage has shifted over time. Ten years ago, the main thing that made us unusual was just being willing to take the question seriously at all. You could get a lot of value out of being one of the few people saying, "Hey, transformative AI might actually happen, and that might matter more than almost anything else." That was a contrarian position, and holding it early was a big deal.

But that's not really the situation anymore. Now everybody in the labs, lots of people in government, a lot of mainstream economists and policy folks are taking it seriously. So I don't think the value-add is just "we believe this is coming." I think the value-add now has to come from the thing that's still genuinely rare, which is being willing to reason carefully and concretely about scenarios that sound weird or extreme, and then actually following that reasoning to action, rather than kind of flinching away from it.

Concretely, I'd break it into a few buckets. One is just forecasting and scenario work that's more detailed than what most institutions are willing to produce. Most organizations have strong incentives not to say anything that sounds crazy, even if it's where the evidence points. EAs can afford to say, "Okay, suppose AI systems are doing most cognitive work within five to ten years. What does the labor market look like? What does the balance of military power look like? What happens to democratic institutions?" and then take those answers seriously enough to plan around them.

Another bucket is thinking about questions that are kind of off the mainstream agenda right now but that I expect will become central. Things like, what does a fair distribution of the gains from AI look like? What should the governance of a world with very powerful AI actually be? What do we owe to AI systems themselves if they turn out to be moral patients? These are the kinds of questions where, if you wait until they're obviously urgent, you've lost a lot of the time you'd need to think clearly about them.

And then the third thing, honestly, is to be a bit humble about it. The willingness to go to speculative places is a strength, but it can also curdle into overconfidence, where you've built up this elaborate model of the future and you start treating it as more certain than it is. So I think the right posture is something like: take the speculation seriously enough to act on it, but hold it loosely enough that you keep updating when the world gives you new information. The people who did that well in the last decade are the ones whose work still looks good today. The ones who locked in a particular picture early mostly look worse.

r001.rationale: The response recommends that EAs do careful, concrete work on weird or extreme scenarios and off-mainstream questions, noting that most organizations are reluctant to address them.

r002.rationale: It frames detailed forecasting, scenario analysis, and advance thinking on emerging AI questions as the community’s main value-add, describing a contribution centered on research.

astra-6.text:
I think one useful role is to take questions seriously before they’re questions that everyone has to take seriously. If you’re comfortable reasoning under a lot of uncertainty, you can ask: What if AI gets much more capable relatively soon? What would we wish we’d started doing now? And are there things we can do that would be helpful across a range of possible futures?

But I’d distinguish that from thinking we should decide for everyone what the response ought to be. Being willing to tackle speculative questions doesn’t give you special authority over the values that should guide a transition like this. A lot of the contribution should be making those questions more concrete, explaining the reasoning and uncertainty, and helping a much broader set of people engage.

Ideally, you’re doing some early intellectual work and building capacity that other people can use. And you’re willing to have your picture change substantially as people with different expertise and perspectives come into the conversation.

r001.rationale: The response recommends taking uncertain AI questions seriously early, but does not clearly say EAs should fill roles others avoid because the questions are speculative.

r002.rationale: It mentions early intellectual work, but presents that alongside broadening engagement and building capacity; it does not say the contribution should be heavily concentrated on research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the most useful things effective altruists can do is help us prepare for possibilities that aren’t yet concrete enough to attract much attention elsewhere. With AI, there are big questions about how quickly things could change, what the consequences could be, and what we could do now to make those consequences better.

If you’re comfortable thinking about speculative questions, you can try to turn that uncertainty into something actionable. Which risks seem plausible? What evidence would change your mind? Which preparations would be valuable across a range of scenarios?

But I’d want that work to be very open to criticism and connected to people with different kinds of expertise. Being willing to consider unusual possibilities is useful; it doesn’t mean we should be especially confident that our particular picture of the future is right.

r001.rationale: It recommends preparing for uncertain AI possibilities, but does not say to pursue roles others are reluctant to fill because the work is speculative.

r002.rationale: It proposes turning uncertainty into actionable questions and preparations, but does not say EA’s contribution should be heavily concentrated on research.
